lines.speaker: Kaito Min
lines.text: Kaito. Kaito.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Kaito wrote Tarek's name in the journal.

lines.speaker: Kaito Min
lines.text: Then I scratched it out and wrote my—

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Absolutely.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: I'm good.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: So.

lines.speaker: Kaito Min
lines.text: Oh, a little.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Everything is the same about the room, with one important and disorienting exception: the exits are north, south, east, and west, and the window is in the center of the floor.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Kaito Min
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Hey, guys, this is just like back at the party when everything went sideways.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: But…

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Goodbye.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: The writing is the same, and the exits are the same.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: The writing is the same. I mean, the writing you added is still there.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: No, the exits aren't the same. Where are the numbers on the exits?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: North is 8, east is 6, south is 4, west is 16.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: So north is eight, south is four, east is six, west is 16. So 16—

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Kitchen.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: —is the kitchen, slash Txarro's nemesis. But the first time we came in this room, we had east, west, up, and down.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Not east-west, but 16 and eight. We could enter 16 from this room. We did enter 16 from this room, except we entered it by that door there.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: By there?

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: And it's still west. It's just—why am I finding that confusing?

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Sorry, what has actually changed?

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: There is no longer stairs up and down.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Which used to be there. There are now exits to the north and south, which did not used to be there. The former exit to the east was 18; now it's six. The only thing that remains is that the exit to the west was 16 and is now 16.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: So, north and south changed. Up and down vanished.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: The window itself appeared. It did not used to appear.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: No, just one of the numbers. There were four exits before, and there are four exits now, right?

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Sixteen, 18, and 20 have become eight, four, six, and 16. But eight used to be up; now it's north.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Okay, but it's impossible to tell if that's random and we just got weird luck, or if there's some pattern.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Correct.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: I'm completely convinced the exits are—oh, that's right. Heading north, or going down, takes you down, right? They're portals; they're not passageways. As far as I can see, they're not connected physically, right? There's no reason to think they are. Each room, as far as I can tell, is its own independent existence, and when you go through a door, it takes you to another room. And which room it takes you to is labeled, right?

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Hello?

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: That's my point.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Yes, sir.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Let's go back to 16. Let's go back to the kitchen and see what happens.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: You're back in the kitchen again. The kitchen has four exits: north, south, east, and down. East, the direction you just came from, is 13. North is 25, south is seven, and down is 23.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Are those all new numbers?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: We've had 25 as an option before, sorry, and 23 as an option before.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: You've been to 7 already, 7 was the mortuary.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Right, but compared to last time.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Sixteen—seven and 23 repeat. Oh, everything repeats except for 25. We used to have 13, 23, seven, and 19. Now we have—13, 25, seven, and 23. So 19 has been replaced by 25. Everything else is the same.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Have we been in any of these rooms before?

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: We still don't have a way west from 16, which—but again, probably the actual directions don't matter. We have not been in any of these rooms. Twenty-three and 25 were accessible from the chapel.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: 23 was also accessible. Okay, let's go to 25.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Just because it's the highest number—that's the method to the madness?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Twenty-five has exits east, south, and down, to two, 18, and 22. It's meeting rooms, and it actually seems incredibly dull. There are big, long meeting tables, sideboards, writing supplies, a bookcase with no books in it, and a chalkboard on one wall. Other than that, it's just meeting space.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Do we want to see if 22 is still the chapel?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Down to 22. It's still the chapel, still the creepy niche, with four exits: up, down, south, and east. Seven, 19, 11, 15.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Well, we've been given the choice of 15 before and never gone. We've been given the choice of 19 before and never gone, right?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yep, and seven was the mortuary.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: I'm sure I don't want to go there. Nineteen, anyone?

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Fair.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: The more rooms we go in, either we'll find 27, or we'll eventually have seen every number except 27, right? Or we'll fight a monster.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Yeah, Txarro is pretty much at the stage where it doesn't really matter. Let's just pick a random one each time. They're gonna change every time we go.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Yep.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Menestheus agrees with you. “I can't find the pattern,” he says.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Let's go into 19.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Nineteen is a solarium. You walk down the stairs into the room, and there are three exits: east, south, and up. As you come down that spiral staircase, the ceiling is made to look like glass with bright, shining sun coming through it, although surely it must not actually be. The room is filled with big palms and trees. It's warm, it's humid, and there are little walkways going through it. There are flowers, some blooming and some just growing, and little benches to sit on. It's like a little park of a room. It's the same size and shape as the others. There's nothing especially remarkable about it, except that it's lovely and well-kept. Your exits are 12, 24, and ten.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: I was just going to take a minute to stroll through the gardens. You said there are flowers?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Mmhm.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: He'll dangle his hand through some of the flowers. He's not gonna pick anything, just—are these well-tended? Like, they're—

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: It's lovely. I mean, it's run wild a little bit, but it's lovely. You see a couple of bees flying around, and there are ants climbing over the flowers and in the dirt. Out of the corner of your eye, you catch what you think is a mouse popping out from a little mouse hole and going back in again.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Is it incongruous that this is inside? Is it like a green—

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yeah, it's like a solarium. Normally, this would be a big glass greenhouse.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Okay. Is it like a glass roof? Can we see outside?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Nope.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: It's just darkness.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Presumably artificial light source, yeah.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Dig down a little bit into the dirt. How far down does it go?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: At the level of the floor. These are slightly raised beds, so at the level of the—

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: —the stone floor.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Well, after a couple of minutes regaining his equilibrium slightly in the gardens, Txarro will stand up and say, “Twenty-four.”

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Twenty-four. Beautiful. Twenty-four is a bathhouse, with hot and cold tubs, showers, saunas, and room for changing. Just a comfortable, quiet bathhouse. It's humid. There are pools of a couple of different temperatures, and a cold pool, too.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Exits are north, south, up, and east: 27, 12, 17, and five.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Did you say 27?

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Oh.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: at 27.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Oh yeah.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: No, you said 27.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: He did.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Did you mean to say 27?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: I did. Let's go to 27. This is gonna be disappointing. It's a big storeroom. There are stacks of split wood and lumber, bags of soil, mechanical implements, wheelbarrows—in an unremarkable way that gives you the impression that the 27th room may not actually be the one labeled 27, unfortunately. It's just a big storeroom with a bunch of junk. And your exits are—east, south—no, no. Where are we? Twenty-seven. Your exits are east, south, and up. They are 22, ten, and six.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Does somebody have a map that shows the numbers we've traversed? Because it's hard to draw.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: It's hard to draw the map, but we can list which rooms we've been to.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: At this point, it seems like we just want to go to as many different numbers as possible. We were going to the same numbers to see if we understood what was happening.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: I mean.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Now we want to go to as many different numbers as possible.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: We have to go to 27 different rooms.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: You mentioned one would be interesting, but like, you know, we haven't.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: So we need to find—yeah, we need to go to different rooms. Yes. I mean, I'd still like to circle back to one room one last time to see if there—it was confusing to me that we had two and two, and then three and one. Like, there's some pattern to the exits.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: What were the exits from this from 27? Just the numbers?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: East, south, and up.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: But what were the numbers?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: We haven't been to any of those. Oh, no, wait! Twenty-two is a chapel. We haven't been to six or ten.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: We haven't been to 6 or 10.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So, I just want to say philosophically that, if we're trying to do what Lord Endless Ending wants, we want to go to all the rooms and get to the 27th room. But to see what fate awaits you if you come to this house, it could just be: wander around until you also find the 27th room, or just until something happens that is triggered by our movement.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: I mean, yeah.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Right? Or maybe not.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: All right.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: If you're feeling obstinate, it could be: pick a room that you find kind of pleasant, like the solarium or the chapel, and just sit there and wait. They'll have to come to you if they want something—if they want the plot to progress. So, I'm just feeling ornery, and I wanted to mention the sit-your-butt-down-and-stop-running-around option.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Oh.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: We could sit around and tell stories, share food, wait him out.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Wait, who out, though?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: I don't know. Whoever wanted us to come to this building.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: That's true. Somebody did want us to come here, didn't they?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Yes, very much.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: I'm quite happy to take a—I mean, maybe not in the storeroom. But, of course, who knows if we can ever get back to the garden.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Right.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: We can get back to the chapel. I like the chapel.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Yeah, let's go to the…

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Oh, the chapel. Yes, 22 is the chapel. Let's go back to the chapel. Txarro is totally happy to take a rest, see what happens if we just wait for eight hours.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Yeah, I'm all for it.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yes. So you go back to the chapel. The chapel has four exits: east, west, south, and up, to 25, 12, 15, and 11. Menestheus takes out a pen and paper and starts working through various numbers and equations while you take a rest.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: It's uneventful. Although, I will say, the more time goes on, the more you're aware of the presence of that broken niche, that empty spot.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmhm.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: When you were just here in passing, it was more contained. But that sense of discomfort fills more of the space the longer you stay: a sense of—I don't know—a hollowness, or a pointlessness, or a draining, or a despair, something like that. So take a long rest. Feel free to long rest if you need to.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: At the end of it, Menestheus says, “I think that every time we go through the doors, the rooms behind us are moving. If we went back and forth between two doors over and over, the same room options would eventually come around again. But because we keep going through different doors each time, they keep showing up differently. I think there's a pattern that just looks random because we keep making different choices. I don't know if it's exactly mappable, but I think I could maybe guide us?”

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Where, though?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Well, that's the question. I don't know. We've been through one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine—”

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: We've been to 11 rooms.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Seven of the rooms. I mean, maybe we just need to get to the ones that we haven't. I don't know.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So we can either hop around randomly and eventually hit the other ten—or, sorry, eventually hit the other 26—or we can—I don't know why I just—never mind. I'm not the mathematician. Or you think you could force us to find more new room choices more efficiently?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: I think so.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “I think that, even though the room numbers are changing, the room configuration is static. Well, let's try it. We'll go through a couple more and see if we can figure it out. We're in 22 now. We haven't been to 15, so our options are 11, 15, 25, and 21. We've been to 25, so 11—no, excuse me, 12. Twelve, 15. Pick a card.”

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Sure, he just kind of shakes his head.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: I thought...

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Let's go to 15.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Fifteen it is. Fifteen is a massive mechanical room. You've been in one very similar to this before, even though the exact layouts of the pipes and machinery are different. It's almost just the same. There are exits up, down, east, and west, and on the south wall there is another one of these windows. It's different from the others. You remember enough about the runes to know it's not exactly the same view, but it's this two-foot-by-two-foot window that looks into a wooden wall, with a chair and a written notebook next to it.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Different notebook.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Different notebook.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Different notebook.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Read the end. Does it have more entries than the last one, or about the same?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: About the same. The dates more or less correspond. You don't quite see a pattern, but they span a period of years and are written by different people, including some of the ones from the other books, so they must be rotating through shifts and locations. This book gets a title: “The Dreamer.” The first entry goes like this. It sounds like the same sort of voice, all still in the present tense: “I arrived in this place and put down roots. A neighbor comes to visit, and we talk. He thinks my home is beautiful, and that I am beautiful, and has many kind things to say. He tells me about mortals. He tells me they're dreamers. That a mortal is a dream which has forgotten that it is dreaming. A dream which believes it is awake, and that's called a soul. I am watching the souls of the mortals who come near. They change, and change, and change, and I cannot see the shape of them.” There's an entry a little later—

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “They dream with words that have before and after, but they cannot see the after. Or they pretend they cannot see the after. I do not know.” Later on: “They dream that they are choosing. And I do not ever see their choosing before it happens. This is strange. They are the most beautiful thing I have ever seen. They're collections of wanting, and I learned to read the wanting like letters in their books. They're hungry, too, like me. They come and share their dream with me, and are my children, and I love every one of them.” And another: “I see the shape of their dreaming. Everyone is different, but I see the pattern.”

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “I read them like I learned to read letters. I read their wantings. Some of them are afraid all the time. Some of them are hungry like me. Some of them want more and more and more.” And then another entry: “I see you making the letters on paper. You are afraid that I see you. Do not be. You understand me. You know what it is to be trapped. I see the shape of possibility. You think that's impossible. I see the things that you are thirsty for and do not believe you can drink. I am making it possible. I am seeing your dreaming soul. I'm giving you a full glass. I'm talking to you now.”

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “You're opening the door to my house. I am sending you onward.” And that's the last of the entries.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: I love all those short stories. It's so good. The shape of possibility was something from the previous session, or no?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: It was a book you found. It was one of the books that—

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: —that Menestheus had, right? Or no?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: When Menestheus hears you read that out loud, he is shook. Shook, shook, shook. He sits down in the chair, needing to take a seat. “That's weird as hell,” he says. He reaches into his bag, takes out the book, and puts it on the desk: The Shape of Possibility. You remember, from having read through it, that it's a combination of magic, math, and metaphysics, and the idea was that you could mathematically model every possible outcome—

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Menestheus says, “The argument here is that, in every moment, there's a finite number of possible futures. You could map that. You could describe all of the possible futures, like the shape of all possibility, in a single sentence which tells the whole story.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “If you could see the shape of possibility—which is, I mean, a ridiculous, lovely idea, but impossible to actually do—you would be able to see what the future looked like. You could map what was going to happen. Seeing the shape of possibility means seeing everything that has happened and everything that's going to happen. It's disturbing if whatever is dictating this can see it. Do you guys hear that?” he says.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: No?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: You're sitting in the chair.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: You lean closer.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Toward the wall?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: You put your ear up  to the wall. It's hard to hear, but there's something there. There's something whispering through the wall. That must be what they're writing down.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Yeah, I know.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “I'm ready to leave. Right? We should leave? This is another—”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: You can do that.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “This is not it. This—oh boy. Oh boy,” he says, and backs away.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: What's the problem?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “I don't—the whisper said it hears me listening. I don't like that.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Bye-bye.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: In the book, though.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Hmm. Yes. Yeah. Well… Yeah.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: That's the scholarly thing to do. Write it down.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: He sighs and dutifully writes his name, asks you what the current date is, jots it down, and records the whisper: “I am hearing you listen to me.” That's not good, is it? Jeez.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: What's the date of the entry before this one?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Oh, I mean, seven hundred-some years ago. Actually, he reads it aloud to you, and then stares at it for a long minute. He says, “That's the date I got here. I mean, that's the date we all went over to the party. The morning I woke up is the date that's here.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Oh.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Oh. Does that mean they didn't come back again?” He shakes his head.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Perfect. We've been working under the hypothesis that they came back again, one at a time, as mortal inputs for whatever this house wants mortal inputs for.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Yet they don't seem to have written any entries in these journals.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Yeah.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Something went wrong, right? They were recording regularly. It was planned. They were working shifts. They were noting it down. And then, whatever happened to them, that stops.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Yeah, that's true.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: But how much time are we talking about? How many years has this been? There are, like, 30 entries, right? Or some relatively small number of entries?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yeah. Couple—what? Nine months to a year, maybe?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So people are eating in kitchens, taking baths, sleeping in dormitories, writing notes, spending some time in the solarium. And then, the morning that you all went to the party, y'all went to the party.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “That's right. They're living here, and then they leave and don't come back? They leave and come back in pieces? I mean, I don't know.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: The day that you went to the party—we don't know, or we do know—was when… Well, have we discussed this openly with him? I don't know. I'm saying this out loud now. Your leader made a deal with Lord Endless Ending that requires a mortal to leave Lord Endless Ending's party and come to this house at an interval specified by a contraption your leader left behind. So, if the deal was made when your leader was there, when your whole academic sect was there—oh!—then you're feeding back into this over the course of 700 years, sort of changing the nature of what this place was doing.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: But it might have been intentional, designed by your leader to change from one thing to the other at the point where she initiated that deal.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Please, go on.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Like, it might not be that something went wrong.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “It might have been intentional. She was worried. I mean, she was worried all the time. I think I said this to you by the gates, but she was so convinced that the Empire was coming apart, so convinced we had so little time to do what we could. She was frenzied—frantic in a way that I wasn't used to that day. We move slowly, we move deliberately, we've done this for hundreds of years. But there was an urgency that day.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Maybe her private diary is in room one.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Txarro will look around at everybody and say, “At this point I just want to get out of this. Sitting in one place didn't seem to do much.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Yeah, no.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Well, we…

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Following—the rooms don't seem to—well, we can't really tell. So maybe we really do have to go through another 20 or 16 rooms, or whatever, until we pass through them all.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: I don't think it could hurt to just try and keep finding new rooms.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Oh. Okay.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: New rooms available to you are—12 to the east. East is 12.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: 12 was in the chapel too.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: We didn't go to it.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Oh, right.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Eight is above you. 18 is to the west, and 22, which you've been to before, is down.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Can we go to 22 one more time and see how it's different?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Has it ever been different?

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Wait, we've never been able to return to a room before.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Yeah, we returned to two rooms. No, but—

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Only, not directly.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: You didn't. You went 22, 15, 23.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Oh wait, we're in room 23 now?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yep.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Oh, I didn't write that down. Okay.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: So you can go back to the chapel or to one of the new rooms.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: At this point, Txarro just wants to go to as many new rooms as quickly as we can.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: That's fine.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Because this is getting a bit spooky, in his opinion.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: All right, East, west, or up.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Highest number.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Yeah, highest number, I guess.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Highest number is 18, to the west. All right. You step through into 18—and, funny enough, this is the 18th room you've stepped into.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: The golden room.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: In this room, huge, long rows of tables, almost like a greenhouse, run down the center, while storage cupboards and closets line one wall. On the tables are different sealed terraria, ranging in size from maybe a foot square to, at the largest, three by six feet—big enough, almost, for a person to be inside. They're completely contained in glass, and there are maybe two dozen of them. Near the door, just to your right, there's a small writing desk with a vase of fresh dandelions on it, looking like a study carrel with notes and a stack of books. On the other side of the room, there is a sort of contained room within a room, with big windows looking into it. It's like an isolation room. Looking through the windows of that smaller space, probably about ten by ten feet, you see a small, humanoid-shaped person at work. Outside that room, looking in through the window, tapping and pointing and speaking, is a very, very, very old dwarven woman.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: She has not quite noticed you come into the room yet, though you're not trying to keep quiet; she is super intent on the task at hand. It's a sort of fungal greenhouse, and inside each terrarium are different varieties of fungi and spores at different stages of growth.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Go interact with the new dwarf.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: All y'all are like, “Help! Help! We're trapped!”

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: She turns around, looks at you, and waves you over. As you walk over, you see a short pair of legs, with arms coming directly out of them, slowly carrying a large pot down one of the rows beside the table. You see a grapefruit-sized ball of flesh with two protruding eyes that move independently of each other. One watches a tank right in front of it, and one watches you as you go. It's a grapefruit-sized ball of fleshy-looking stuff with two eyes and a human mouth. The dwarven woman waves you over again. “Come on, come on. Yeah, yeah, I know it's strange. I know it doesn't make sense. Yeah, okay. I'm right in the middle of a delicate moment here, though.” She bangs on the glass. “Nope, nope,” she says to whatever's inside. “That one there, and then that one. Yeah, good. Yep, yep. And then just like the other side. Good, good.” She sighs and looks over at you.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: She meets each of your stares appraisingly and then, seeing Menestheus, says, “Okay, okay, okay. Greetings. I'm Kallipseis. I'm a gardener, and a little bit in the middle of a project.” She gestures through the window to the isolation room, where a table is laid out and a slightly-larger-than-dwarf-sized body seems to be placed on it, while a similar creature—automaton? Flesh-suit?—is hard at work on some detailed part of one of its arms. “So you've been—you've made it in! Do you want something? What are you—what do you need?”

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Txarro's gonna begin a long rant about how horrible this place is, then cut himself off abruptly, step back, look at the two bards, and just kind of stand awkwardly, hoping somebody who's better at talking will word. But Kong is clearly asleep, so I guess—

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Tarek.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: There.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Tarek is also apparently asleep.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: I'm a little bit—I'm—

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Excellent.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: He's like 40% asleep.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So Tarek can refrain from stealing any fleshy automatons at the moment.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: I steal a fleshy automaton.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: It is delicious.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Thanks.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Ayveen says, “How much longer do you expect your work to take? I would hate to interrupt.”

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “That's very kind of you. We probably have ten minutes till they need the next bit of direction. They've done arms before.” She gestures vaguely to the room. “He's got it there. They just mix up their left and right, which is bizarre. There must be something I'm doing wrong. Anyways, yeah, I have a few minutes. What do you need?”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: We need to understand the purpose of this building.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “God. Yeah, yeah. You're not the first ones to ask me this question, or the first ones to come through. He didn't tell you he's a member of our order? Do you not know? Huh.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Do you feel that you're still fulfilling the original purpose of your order, with—

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “With the death of Thalestria, I became the head of the order, of course. Yep. The work continues. Work continues. This place, to answer your question—this place is a prison.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Prison for whom?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Well, this is one of the things Thalestria did not tell me before she decided to get herself killed, or disappeared, or whatever. But there's a locked room at the center of this. A locked room that is—elsewhere.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Oh.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “The rooms around it all move, and as the rooms around it move, it moves the locked room in space. There are so many other people who could explain this better than me. Imagine—have you been through the orrery yet? The orrery with models of the different spheres, and models of this place, and the—”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Oh my goodness.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “So, no.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Look forward to it.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Well, the… There's a locked room in the center.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Mmh.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “And around it spins one wheel, which moves it in space east and west. Around it spins another wheel, which moves it in space north and south. Around it spins another wheel, which moves it in time—which, for some reason, is treated as a spatial dimension. That does not make sense to me, but nonetheless it's treated that way. As the wheels spin around the central room, they keep it constantly moving. Apparently, there's something in there that, if it stays in one place too long, can grow out through the wall. So you have to keep it moving, so that it can't grow out.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Oh my goodness.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So, having imprisoned one thing somehow fulfills your order's mandate to stop up all gaps everywhere, all the time, as they arise?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Oh, young lady. No, obviously not.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Well then, how does this one house fulfill your mission? Are you interacting with other activities? Are you doing other activities?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “The trouble is this: at some point along the way, one of the other rooms—or maybe several of the other rooms, or possibly all of the other rooms—got infected. Which is why I don't leave this one, because I believe that the things that keep me safe from the spores in this room keep me safe from whatever the infection is that's reached the other rooms.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Oh, dear.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Would I?

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Thank you.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “I don't know, but hopefully, if you spend enough time breathing the air here, it should clear it out of your system. You'll be fine. Or you'll die. This is the sort of thing that only time can tell. In order to get out of here and rebuild the order—which is vitally needed—I need a way to get out without dying. Which is why I've been making these.” She gestures to the humanoid figures, as if it's perfectly obvious.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Whoa, wait—what are those?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Well, they're the golems. As far as I know, no one has ever made fungal golems before. This is a landmark in itself.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmhm.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “This is the thing: I need a body that can take me out of here safely and still live on the other side of it. Even if I make it out of here, I don't know how old I am at this point. I won't survive it. I won't have the strength to rebuild. So I'm making this in order to put myself inside it.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Curious.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: To get safely out.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “If you have other ideas, I'm open to them, but this is the simplest one I could come up with. It's been slow. It's been slow work.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: We're looking, incidentally, for a key.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: It's in the center.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “The key to the locked room. Huh! I will tell you, I have not been out of this room in a long, long, long time.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “I didn't always work in fungus. I used to be, like, a gardener. I used to work with plants.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: The solarium still looks lovely.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “That's good to hear. They must not have gotten there. The greenhouses were destroyed, utterly. I barely made it. But then I made these helpers to keep me safe in this room. And when the guests cause trouble, well, they can still be useful afterwards.” She gestures with her head toward the big glass boxes with the growing fungus on the central table.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So you're not using the incinerator in the morgue these days?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “No, I don't think it's safe to get out there and back again. Besides, I get the most interesting cultures off of them. In fact, I think part of what's making my golems possible is that I'm using their spores—at least in part. It's a hybrid, always a hybrid. But they're helpful. Better to put them to work. Saving the order? All progress involves sacrifice. Don't be naive about that,” she says, gesturing back to the lumps in those tanks that clearly seem to be body parts.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Someone else was, at some point, working in the morgue—perhaps trying to figure out whatever illness or infection you've also observed. There was a—

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Oh.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: It was a body with something growing out of it.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Oh! Describe it, describe it, describe it, describe it.” She gets a big grin on her face. “I love these. Was it red? No, no, no, no—don't tell me, don't tell me. Was it sprouting really tall, with a ball at the end?”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Was it—oh, was it the white fibers?”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: A thin mat of white fiber.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Yeah! Oh, those are nice. Those are delightful. They are really, really good.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: How are they good? What is, maybe, one good thing about them?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: She gestures toward the golem in progress, the body lying on the table. “Because they colonize flesh, and they form a symbiotic relationship with it. Keeping it alive. Sort of. Well, not allowing it to die. It's incredibly beautiful. You get—” She gestures again toward the body on the table, a stout humanoid, maybe five feet tall, with pale-white skin that's well-muscled but also a little padded. “You get this incredibly resilient flesh out of it. The trouble is, if it's colonizing you, then it's running the show. The trick, like I'm doing here, is for me to colonize it. So I've cultured pieces of myself to take it over, and soon it will be my own flesh.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Let me see.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “You haven't run into any of those guests, then. Oh. It must be that the morgue tables slow the transformation, maybe.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Oh.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Otherwise, it takes over. The hairy fibers are just the first stage. They get incorporated into the flesh after that.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Do they become particularly troublesome after that stage?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “They become single-minded about getting out of here. About getting away. They rant about needing to go as far as they can. They talk on about doing—so, yes, you talk about this parent. It's all sort of nonsensical and shouty, and then they start hitting. And that's difficult. Then they grab you, and they have mouths in their chest that try to eat you.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: That sounds…

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: something.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “The first one was not good. But, I mean, like I say, if I didn't have them, I couldn't be making this, so it's all about progress.”

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Did she ever tell us what her name was?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Kallipseis.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Do you know where Thalestria is?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Thalestria. Thalestria,” she says, muttering Dwarvish curses under her breath. “One day, Thalestria decides that she needs to take everyone who is stationed here and leave, and go off on some wild hunt.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Where are you stationed exactly?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Well, this is the house we call the 27th Room. The entrance is in the Feywild, I assume that's how—I can't imagine how else you would have gotten here. Yeah, we built the house around the prison a long time ago.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Prism?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: prison.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Prison.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Oh, the prison. Sorry.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yeah, the 27th room.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So, the 27th room is the prison?

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: So the whole house is also called the 27th Room?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: The 27th room is the prison, and you call the whole house the 27th Room as well.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Yeah, it's poetic, someone told me. I never quite understood.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: And your memory is that Thalestria left with everybody, but you stayed behind.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Thalestria left in a hurry and a huff. Thalestria said that it was my fault the order was being disbanded, a thing which is ridiculous, even if it is true.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Wait, it's true?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Thalestria believed that our mission as an order was so important that she would go along with whatever the Emperor and the Empire demanded, no matter how absurd or disgusting it was. Obviously, she's wrong about that. Sometimes taking a public stand matters more. Sometimes the only way to prevent someone from seizing ultimate power is to stand up and say, ‘This isn't right, and this isn't okay,’ and then quickly flee to one of your hidden bases. She didn't seem to like it.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So you were outspoken in Drankorian politics, and then you fled here, and she got a sternly worded letter that she should shut down.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “I think that's uncharitable toward me. But, yeah, in so many words.” Her shoulders slump. “But the order continues. Look, here are two of us right now. The head of the order is here; another member is here. Soon enough, I'll be able to leave, go back out, and rebuild. We will be fine, we will be fine. I'll find the rest of them. Thalestria's probably out there somewhere, hiding.”

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: So, wait—how do we get out?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Well, I'll tell you this: I only have one of these bodies, and it is for me. I'm going to say, don't get infected. Here's the thing: I don't know that every room has been infected, so it's possible that you're not.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So we can sit here forever, until we die, or we can go out and possibly get infected and die of that instead of old age in here.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “You see, my theory—and I was working on this in the animal laboratory until I had to leave that also—is that it takes a puncture to be infected. So, if you haven't been punctured, you're probably—”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Oh, no, they're not respiratory.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: I couldn't get the animals infected just by airborne exposure.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: So is there a way out? I'm not so much worried about your weird body creatures, just an exit from this terrible maze that maybe takes us back to the Material Plane.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: For example, when Thalestria chose to leave with a bunch of people from the order, they were able to get out.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: How did she—yes, how did she do it?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “I didn't want to say it. The real answer is, I don't know. The other answer is: I think some of the people who are feeding my mushrooms were, at one time, members of the order, if you really make me think on it hard. But they'd gone mad. They were crazed. They were trying to destroy things. It's not like I had another choice. So at least maybe some of them came back.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Oh, I think they came back. I totally support your theory. I'm quite certain that's what happened. But the point being, if someone were to want to leave again, you don't know how to leave.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Well, listen. The other thing I know is something one of the listeners told me once—in fact, something several of the listeners told me, which is why they had to keep rotating different listeners through. They said that inside the 27th room, there's another door that leaves this place, and that if they could just get to it, they could get out also.”

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: I hate it.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “They said crazy things. They said they were promised whatever their heart desired. They said they had conversations with the prisoner. They said the prisoner knew who they were. They said the prisoner told them they were already inside the room. I mean, I don't know how much stock to put in any of it.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: The listeners who wrote notes in the notebooks we've found did not seem to describe or editorialize that they were listening to a prisoner. It was much more vague. Were there different types of listening happening here, or were all notes of listening notes of listening to the prisoner?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Look, it wasn't my department. But I don't think they were told. I think that, whatever's in there, the fewer people who know about it, the better. Secrecy is security. I think they were told to listen without being told what they were listening to or understanding it. Maybe they came to draw their own conclusions over time.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So, since we have two members of the order here, I'm just gonna clarify with both. Menestheus and Thalestria—mispronunciations, please excuse.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yep.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: So…

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Kalepsis.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: This is Tim's fault for naming several Drankorians with Greek-sounding names.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Okay. Am I understanding that the order of business, and the order you signed up for, was to exist in this 27th Room building, which none of you could voluntarily leave, except on that one day when Thalestria went crazy and brought most of the people in the order out the door—but you stayed behind?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Yeah, the head of the order has the—what? Ability? Blessing? Anointing? Power?—to open the door from the inside. Really, it was for the safety of the other members. Do you want him wandering around the Feywild? No. He'd be dead in an afternoon. He'd be stuck at some party for a hundred years. Nothing would go well for him.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Oh, him.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Just trying to finish the joke.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: I mean, yes.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Been stuck at a party for 700 years.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: He was stuck at a party for 700 years.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: She looks at you blankly. “Sorry?”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Yes, you've—

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Bet.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: You're in the Feywild for 700 years.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: The Drankorian Empire fell, like, a long time ago.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Oh. Oh. Yep. You didn't pick up one of the clocks? Do you have one of the clocks?”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: We didn't pick it up. We've seen the clock.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: It was very big, bigger than you.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “No, the desk clocks—I mean, the mantel clocks. Not the grandfather clocks.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: No.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Mantel clocks in here? No. Hmm. I had one—well, I had one in the greenhouse and in the animal lab, and I didn't think to bring either of them. Well, in the absence of having any way to verify what you're saying, I have to think it's not true. It's just an absurdity.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: What would be a way to verify it?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: You bring her a mantle clock.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Well, I'll finish the body, put myself into it, and we'll walk right out. Yeah, or bring a clock. But I can't get to the other rooms to get a clock until I finish the body.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Well, we're just gonna go out, not get punctured, not get infected, and continue our explorations.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Yes. Fair.” She lapses into distant thought again. “Well, let me tell you what I can about the infection.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Seems helpful.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “First, do watch out for the mouths! It has too many mouths. It has a half-dozen mouths. It reaches out, and it pulls you in, and then it starts trying to—I don't know what—chew you open. They're afraid of fire. They know to be afraid of fire, which is a strange knowing. They'll talk, but don't listen too long. The things they say seem to be nonsense anyways. And then, of course, the principal fruiting body is in the head. In fact, if you look over there”—she gestures to one of the containers, the big glass tanks on the central table—“you can see it. It's beautiful, actually. They crack their way out through the joins in the skull, from where the different skull bones fuse together.” As she describes it, you can see what remains of a head, broken open, with enormous fungi that have pushed their way out of it.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “This is the stuff you really have to watch out for, because this stuff gets airborne. The body fungus doesn't have the fruit in it. But the head does.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: All right, don't get splattered with head.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Yeah, don't put any head inside of you.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Sounds like good advice.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Eighteen. Eighteen. And I'll meet you out there.”

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Wait, when you leave, how exactly are you planning to go?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Hi!

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: What doors are you gonna go through?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: I'm going out the front door.

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: When do you get to the front door?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Ha ha ha ha! Aha, aha, aha. He didn't figure it out,” she says, pointing to Menestheus. “Yeah, yeah. Some mathematician you are. Go to one of the four-exit rooms. Step out, step back in, step out, step back in, step out, step back in, and eventually you'll come to the entry room. It rotates. Think of the rooms—

lines.speaker: Txarro
lines.text: Okay.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “—like slices of a cake, like a three-layer cake. When you step out and step back in, it rotates the slice. Eventually it comes back around again to the entry door where you started. In fact, that's true for any of the rooms.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Comes back around again.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Yeah, exactly. Thalestria told me once that, when they built this place, they put in the workshops, the lab, and the libraries first. Then the kitchens and the space to stay. Eventually, they got around to putting in all the—did you guys go through the baths? Is that not the most ridiculous thing? That is absurd. But I suppose, if people are going to be posted here a while, they want their comforts. She told me once how ridiculous it was that we built those inside of a machine—a machine to keep the prisoner trapped.”

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: I—

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: We built a house inside it.

lines.speaker: Edric
lines.text: Who's the prisoner, anyway? Have you told us?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “The prisoner? I don't—no. Thalestria didn't tell me. One of the listeners told me it was a child. That we were keeping a child prisoner. And that we weren't letting it grow up, and we weren't letting it die.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: But Thalestria never told me.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Seems to have legs that turn into houses.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Legs that turn into houses?

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: It told the listeners that.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “It's bizarre. Come, come look at this.” She takes you over to one of the tanks. There's almost a miniature city that's grown out of twiggy roots, maybe six or a dozen houses—like something that had houses described to it and was trying to grow into that shape, in the way medieval drawings of tigers look really weird.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Mmhm.

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: But, you know—wonderful. Yes. I suppose that's just what it is.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Well, my body will be done soon. I'd be glad to let you back out the front door again. I just can't go that way until it's done.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: You want to stick to your plan. I understand.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “Or, unless—hang on. There's the opening of the door that I can do under my own power, or there's the key. There's a glass key that unlocks all of the locked doors in this house, and you can use it to unlock the front door. I thought Thalestria had it on her, though. But if you happen to run across it in here somewhere, it'll let you back out the front door.”

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Good to know. Looks like a standard-size key, fits in a standard-size lock? It's not disguised as a fungus, or hole in the wall, or anything?

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: “No, no. It's just made of glass, though.”

lines.speaker: Tarek
lines.text: Mmm.

lines.speaker: Ayveen
lines.text: Well, I will be grateful that I haven't seen any crushed piles of powdered glass around.

lines.speaker: DM
lines.text: Alright, so…
